Synthesis: An equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi ingot was produced by arc-melting pure elements in a vacuum induction furnace. To refine grains, the ingot was cold-rolled to 50% and subsequently annealed at 1150 ◦C for 1.5 h. The samples for spalling experiments were machined from the annealed plate and polished with fine SiC papers. Hydrogen was introduced into the samples by using a cathodic electrochemical charging technique in 0.5 mol L􀀀 1 H2SO4 + 1 g L􀀀 1 CH4N2S (thiourea) solution with a constant current density of 100 mA cm􀀀 2 at 80 ◦C. The hydrogenation time was 48 h, and H-charged samples were immediately immersed in liquid nitrogen until tests were performed.
Refereces: Xie, Z. C., Li, C., Wang, H. Y., Lu, C., & Dai, L. H. (2021). Hydrogen induced slowdown of spallation in high entropy alloy under shock loading. International Journal of Plasticity, 139, 102944.

Synthesis: The materials investigated in this work include disks machined from a bimetallic cylinder consisting of AM GRCop-84 (Cu-8 at. % Cr-4 at. % Nb), which is a powder metallurgy copper alloy developed by the NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) for high temperature applications, and Inconel® 625, a nickel-based superalloy with excellent high temperature mechanical properties. Figure 1(a) shows a sketch (not to scale) of a small section of the right-circular cylinder with a nominal wall thickness of 6.35mm and an outer diameter of ∼221 mm, fabricated via SLM using GRCop-84 at NASA GRC and Inconel® 625 deposited around the outside of the cylinder using EBF3 at the NASA Langley Research Center. The fabricated GRCop-84 inner cylinder, as well as the final bimetallic structure, was hot isostatically pressed (HIP). The microstructure of GRCop-84 has nanoscale Cr2Nb precipitates (up to ∼14 vol. %) that form at the grain boundaries of the copper matrix, which has grain sizes typically around 2–30 μm.36 Inconel® deposited via EBF,3 has a microstructure consisting of a cellular dendritic structure that grows epitaxially in the build direction on the inner GRCop-84 cylinder.34 The deposition process creates a generally wavy and irregular interface between the bimetallic constituents. The two-layered bimetallic samples were machined using wire electrical discharge in the form of disks with a 25.4mm diameter and approximately 5mm thickness.
Refereces: Boddorff, A. K., Jang, S., Kennedy, G., Taminger, K., & Thadhani, N. N. (2022). Spall failure of additively manufactured two-layered Cu–Ni bimetallic alloys. Journal of Applied Physics, 131(17).

Synthesis: Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 (at%) high-entropy alloy was used in this study. The alloy is firstly smelted in a vacuum medium frequency induction furnace and cooled in the furnace. The whole process is carried out under Ar gas protection atmosphere. The induction furnace model is ZG~0.01. The content of elements of the as-cast alloy was determined by the full-spectrum direct-reading plasma emission spectrometer (ICP-OES). In order to obtain samples of different phase content (martensite phase þ matrix phase), the as-cast samples were subjected to the following thermomechanical treatment: (1) Samples were firstly heat-treated at 1173K for 2h and hot-rolling with a 50% deformation (total of 5 times, 10% for each time), and cooled to the room temperature in the air. Then the hot-rolled air-cooled samples were further annealed at 1273K for 2h within an Argon protected atmosphere, and finally quenched in the water to obtain the sample before impact loading (hot-rolling þ quenching, HRQ sample). (2) On the basic treatment of (1), samples were further cold-rolled with a deformation of 40% (total of 8 times, 5% for each time), then annealed at 1173K for 5min, finally quenched in the water (cold-rolling þ quenching, CRQ sample).
Refereces: Yang, Y., Yang, S., & Wang, H. (2021). Effects of the phase content on dynamic damage evolution in Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 high entropy alloy. Journal of Alloys and Compounds, 851, 156883.

Synthesis: The material was consolidated from alloyed powder obtained via SWAP. This process uses a combined gas- and water-atomized powder deposition to produce ultrafine-grained microstructures and super-saturation of alloying elements. According to the manufacturer and related reports on this Mg alloy [6–8], the SWAP process results in powder aggregates having irregular shapes, with a size in the range of 1–5 mm, and a submicrometer- sized grain structure (1 μm or smaller). The as-received powder was subsequently consolidated into billets by cold compaction (at room temperature) and hot-extruded between 573 and 673 K into rectangular bars. The resulting bars had dimensions of 25.4 mm (thickness) × 101.6 mm (width) × 1000 mm (length).
Refereces: Farbaniec, L., Williams, C. L., Kecskes, L. J., Becker, R., & Ramesh, K. T. (2017). Spall response and failure mechanisms associated with a hot-extruded AMX602 Mg alloy. Materials Science and Engineering: A, 707, 725-731.

Synthesis: A rectangular Mg alloy (AZ31B-H24) plate with the dimensions of 152.4 mm × 152.4 mm and a thickness of 12.7 mm was extruded by ECAE through a die using a hybrid 4E route. The 4E route implies that the plate was rotated about the plate normal 180° after the first pass, 90° after the second pass, and 180° after the third pass, and extruded through the die for a total of four passes. The plate processing temperature was varied from 498 K during the first two passes then was dropped to 473 K on the last two passes. The extrusions were performed with a back pressure ranging from 4.14 kPa to 6.89 kPa and the extrusion speed was 4.6 mm/min
Refereces: Farbaniec, L., Williams, C. L., Kecskes, L., Ramesh, K. T., & Becker, R. (2016). Microstructural effects on the spall properties of ECAE-processed AZ31B magnesium alloy. International Journal of Impact Engineering, 98, 34-41.

Synthesis: The triple vacuum arc remelted Ti–45Al–5Nb–B–C at. % gamma TiAl material used in the present investigation was supplied by Plansee AG in the form of 38.1 mm round bars. The gamma TiAl ingots were extruded in two steps at a nominal billet preheat temperature of 1280 °C to a final extrusion ratio 14:1 and a diameter of 38.1 mm. The as-extruded bars had a duplex microstructure with a high volume fraction of lamellar grains, which varied slightly from batch to batch. The lamellar grain size was 20 m; small 4 m gamma grains were found to be present in between lamellar colonies in all batches. A fully lamellar microstructure, with a lamellar colony size of 32545 m, was formed by heat treating the 12.7 mm bars at 1340 °C for 40 min in vacuum followed by furnace cooling. Microstructural investigation, Fig. 1, shows that the material consists of fully lamellar microstructure when the material was sectioned normal to the rod axis. However, a layer of about 4.0 mm thickness at the rod circumference had a near-lamellar microstructure.
Refereces: Shazly, M., & Prakash, V. (2008). Shock response of a gamma titanium aluminide. Journal of Applied Physics, 104(8).

Synthesis: The billets for the preparation of vanadium samples were cut from a 6mm thick plate of vanadium of 99.38% purity containing 0.15% Fe, 0.2% Al, 0.2% Si, and up to 0.01%, 0.001%, 0.03%, and 0.03% N, H, O, and C, respectively. The samples, 2 × 20 × 20mm3 squares, were cut from the billets by electrical discharge machining (EDM) and ground to 0.2 mrad parallelism. Three groups of the samples were prepared. The first group, VA0 in follows, contained undeformed samples. Synthesis: An elemental mixture of tungsten, nickel, and iron powders was isostatically pressed at 207 MPa and room temperature. This pressed material was then sintered in a molybdenum wound furnace at 1793 K in a dry hydrogen atmosphere to prevent oxidation of the elemental powder surfaces. The sintered material was then vacuum- annealed at 1273 K for 10 h to remove the adsorbed hydrogen. The annealed mate- rial was subsequently heated in an inert gas atmosphere to 1373 K and kept at this temperature for 1 h before being water-quenched. The quenched material was then machined into a bar shape and swaged to a 17% reduction in area.
Type of experiment: 10 cm diameter single-stage gas gun facility
Refereces: Dandekar, D. P., & Weisgerber, W. J. (1999). Shock response of a heavy tungsten alloy. International journal of plasticity, 15(12), 1291-1309.
